articles.title: Jillian Michaels urges parents to fight back against Big Tech's 'addictive' grip on kids
articles.summary: Jillian Michaels expressed concerns about screen time for children and called on parents to hold tech companies accountable in Fox Nation's "Toxic 2: A Generation on the Brink."
articles.body: Fitness trainer and media personality Jillian Michaels is urging parents to "keep the pressure on" social media companies, warning about the platforms' allegedly "addictive" algorithms and content. Michaels made the comments during an appearance on "The Faulkner Focus" while promoting her new Fox Nation documentary, "Toxic 2: A Generation on the Brink." Michaels advised parents to limit their children's access to online activities. "You have to do everything you can," Michaels said. "And that means putting parental controls on your kid's phone, period. Take the phone away at night, limit the sites that they can access, have communications with them regularly about the content that they're seeing online. But you also have to be realistic about what they're going to do when they're not with you." CHRIS HANSEN URGES PARENTS TO TEACH CHILDREN ABOUT ONLINE PREDATORS BEFORE ALLOWING INTERNET ACCESS "This is the part where we also have to continue putting pressure on the social media companies to make their algorithms safer for kids," she said. "They created an addictive product, they know it, and we need to keep the pressure on." In the documentary, Michaels examines the risks she says children face in the modern age, including excessive screen time, mental health issues and over-medicalization. "The truth is, a lot of parents probably don't realize the scale of what kids are dealing with today," she said. "From day one, the fragile little bodies and brains of the tiniest and most vulnerable among us are being targeted, treated and toxified from all angles." NATION'S SECOND-LARGEST SCHOOL DISTRICT MOVES TO LIMIT KIDS' SCREEN TIME Michaels is joined by several experts in "Toxic 2: A Generation on the Brink," including psychology researcher Jean Twenge, who argues that individuals who begin using smartphones at an early age are more likely to experience mental health issues later in life. "In some of the best design studies, the heaviest users of social media are about twice as likely to be depressed as lighter non-users," Twenge said. "Even in other studies, you see at least often a 40% or a 50% increase in depression from not using social media to being a heavy user of social media." "Gen Z and Gen Alpha know how bad these technologies can be for them," Twenge added. "They're the ones who came up with phrases like 'chronically online,' which make it sound like a disease, 'brain rot,' that it's bad for your attention span and your focus." FRANCE BECOMES FIRST EU NATION TO BAN SOCIAL MEDIA FOR CHILDREN UNDER 15 Social media companies have faced increasing pressure to be regulated and be held accountable for the potential effects of their platforms. In August, Meta agreed to pay as much as $17.1 billion and implement restrictions on teen accounts to settle claims that it designed Facebook and Instagram to addict children and misled the public about the platforms' safety. Meta denied the allegations. For more on the potential risks personal tech and other issues pose to young children, make sure to watch "Toxic 2: A Generation on the Brink," now streaming on Fox Nation. articles.title: Elon Musk says Tesla will sell 5 million cars by 2030 — math says otherwise
articles.summary: Elon Musk wants Tesla to hit 5 million vehicle deliveries by 2030, but falling sales and a risky Cybercab pivot make that goal nearly impossible.
articles.body: On Tesla’s earnings call Wednesday, Elon Musk made one of his patented pie-in-the-sky predictions that typically sends his fans into paroxysms of ecstasy: 5 million vehicle deliveries by 2030. “We were aiming for 5 million vehicles a year by approximately 2030,” he said. “And I think we’ve got a good shot of achieving that goal.” You’d be forgiven for missing the statement amid the veritable firehose of Musk superlatives — the company’s Terafab chip factory “will be the most valuable building in the world” with “an economic value that’s going to be placed in the top 20 countries” and “Tesla will end up being a majority of all passenger miles on Earth in any country where it is allowed to operate freely” — but nevertheless it’s an important one to clock. For one, it’s an example of Musk quietly downgrading his own projections, considering he said in 2020 that Tesla would sell 20 million cars annually by 2030. And also because I think this one in particular is going to come back and bite him in the ass. Musk’s goal to hit 5 million vehicles sold annually by 2030 would require a complete reinvention of Tesla’s business model, and not in the way he is currently trying to rewrite the company’s mission. After back-to-back delivery declines — falling from a peak of 1.81 million in 2023 to 1.64 million in 2025 — the company would need to sell a shit ton of vehicles to meet that goal. And it neither has the right vehicles nor enough factory space to do so. But this is Tesla we’re talking about, the company that traffics in the impossible. Could Musk pull it off? Well, that depends. Do you think the company will actually sell its flying Roadster to customers? If so, then yes, Tesla can probably do it. After all, Elon would never lie to you, would he? But if you’re one of those people who think the Roadster was a cool demo but an absurdly unrealistic consumer product, then read on. First, let’s take a look at Tesla’s annual delivery numbers. * 2021: 936,172 (+87.2 percent year over year) * 2022: 1,313,851 (+40.3 percent) * 2023: 1,808,581 (+37.7 percent; peak volume) * 2024: 1,789,226 (-1.1 percent; first annual decline) * 2025: 1,636,129 (-8.6 percent; second consecutive drop) Sales volume peaked in 2023, and since then has dropped for two years in a row. So far this year, Tesla has sold 1,324,681 vehicles, meaning it would need to sell 311,448 vehicles in the fourth quarter just to avoid a third straight year of declines. That seems eminently doable, especially given Tesla’s habit of offering aggressive deals toward the end of the year as a way to clear out inventory and boost those final numbers. In all likelihood, Tesla will sell enough vehicles in Q4 to give it a nice bump over its annus horribilis of 2025. (Analysts are predicting 1.82 million for the full year, which would be the company’s best so far.) [Image: So, to explore how Tesla can get to 5 million by 2030, we need to take into account something called compound annual growth rate, or CAGR. This is the percentage by which sales would need to grow every single year to get from where it is now to where Musk wants it to be. You calculate it by taking your target value (5 million) and dividing it by your starting value (1,636,129) to find the overall factor by which Tesla’s sales would need to grow. So the company faces a daunting 25 percent CAGR to get to Musk’s stated goal of 5 million cars sold annually by 2030. Musk would argue this is achievable given Tesla’s current transformation from electric vehicle manufacturer to global leader in AI and robotics. A key pillar in this strategy is the Cybercab and the company’s Robotaxi fleet. If the company is able to successfully launch unsupervised Full Self-Driving in the second quarter of 2027 — which Tesla’s VP for Autonomy Ashok Elluswamy claimed during the earnings call — then demand for Tesla’s vehicles arguably would skyrocket. Moreover, VP for Vehicle Engineering Lars Moravy said that Tesla would try to deliver the first steering-wheel- and pedal-less Cybercabs to customers (likely fleet owners) before the end of the year. If Tesla can create an entirely new sales channel by selling Cybercabs to fleet owners, rather than relying solely on individual retail buyers, then perhaps 5 million cars isn’t so much of a reach. And yet! A closer look at Tesla’s current product lineup reveals some structural deficiencies. Over 96 percent of the company’s sales depend on just two vehicles: the Model 3 and Model Y. Tesla discontinued the Model S and Model X earlier this year to make room at its plant in Fremont, California, for the production of its humanoid robot. The Cybertruck has been a sales flop, missing its initial targets by a wide margin. The Roadster may fly, but the hypercar is a nothingburger with regards to Tesla’s automotive business. (Musk himself admitted the Roadster was a “small potato” project that won’t move the needle financially.) That leaves the Cybercab and the Semi. The latter represents a significant piece of the puzzle. As Tesla ramps up Semi production at its Nevada factory, selling large electric trucks to commercial delivery fleets could give the company a profitable way to ship tens of thousands more heavy vehicles each year, expanding its business beyond consumer cars. But it’s clear from Musk’s statements that he thinks Tesla’s best hope rests with the Cybercab. The chips are stacked against the gilded two-seater. Before Tesla can sell or operate thousands of fully driverless cars on public roads, governments around the world have to adapt to the new technology. Getting government approval takes time and varies state by state and country by country. And Tesla is not the most persuasive company when it comes to creating new rules. Federal regulators are already scrutinizing whether the company skirted the law by rolling out the Cybercab in Austin, Texas. If regulators drag their feet, or if the technology isn’t 100 percent reliable in every city, companies won’t buy Cybercabs in bulk. Instead of selling millions of autonomous taxis to commercial fleets by 2030, Tesla would be left trying to sell traditional cars to individual buyers. But Musk is such a true believer that he abandoned plans for a $25,000 mass-market EV (the so-called “Model 2”) in favor of going all in on the Cybercab. In doing so, he allowed the rest of the world — but especially China — to beat Tesla to the punch. Now we’re seeing Tesla’s market share in Europe and Asia being eroded by affordable models from BYD, Geely, and Xiaomi. Also, Tesla is running headlong into a big factory problem. The company’s current factories can build only around 2.5 million to 3 million vehicles a year. To reach 5 million, Tesla would have to roughly double its factory space or build up to three new Gigafactories, which would take years and require massive spending, new supply chains, and a huge increase in battery production. While Tesla remains a global force, reaching 5 million vehicles without a cheap electric car or regulatory-approved robotaxi network requires a rate of growth that seems utterly divorced from reality. Musk puts on a great show, but when it comes to delivering on his gigantic promises, he often leaves his audience scratching their heads.

articles.title: Amazon renames Kindle Unlimited to Kindle Plus and expands access to audiobooks
articles.summary: Amazon’s Kindle Unlimited is now Kindle Plus. Pricing hasn’t changed, but subscribers will have access to more ebook titles with accompanying audiobooks.
articles.body: The plus-ification of subscription services continues unabated with Amazon becoming the latest company to follow suit with a Kindle Unlimited rebrand. The subscription service is now known as Kindle Plus but will continue to offer unlimited access to a select collection of ebooks, comics, and magazines from the Kindle catalog for $11.99 per month. Thousands of those titles will also still have access to companion audiobooks so you can switch back and forth between reading and listening exactly where you left off, but Kindle Plus will expand that access to include “virtual voice” audiobooks read by AI narrators, according to ZDNet. “The subscription continues to offer the same great reading experience with access to millions of titles, now with the addition of thousands of audiobooks in the U.S. catalog at no extra cost,” Amazon spokesperson Josh Pflug told The Verge in an emailed statement. Kindle Plus will remain a standalone subscription that’s separate from Amazon Prime, and users will still be limited to borrowing up to 20 titles at once, but with no return dates. Amazon is now also allowing authors using its Kindle Direct Publishing platform to make their audiobooks available to Kindle Plus subscribers. Virtual voice audiobooks will automatically be available as new titles are enrolled in KDP Select, but authors can opt-in to AI narrators for previous published titles, too. For authors who prefer a human narrator, audiobooks created using Audible’s Audiobook Creation Exchange (ACX) marketplace will now also be available through Kindle Plus, but starting with subscribers in the US. Amazon plans to expand availability to other markets over time.

articles.title: Tesla driver using Full Self-Driving struck and killed a man crossing I-80
articles.summary: A 71-year-old man has died after he was hit on I-80 by a Tesla the driver said was in Full Self-Driving mode.
articles.body: A 71-year-old man was fatally hit by a Tesla operating in Full Self-Driving (FSD) mode while crossing I-80 in Vallejo, CA around 2:30 AM on Thursday, reports the San Francisco Chronicle. The California Highway Patrol’s statement to media outlets says it reviewed video of the accident from the Tesla’s dashcam, which “showed the Tesla’s brakes being applied as the vehicle steered to the left in an effort to avoid the pedestrian [...] Despite these evasive actions, the right front portion of the Tesla struck the individual.” According to the Chronicle, authorities believe at least one other vehicle struck the pedestrian after the Tesla, but other than the Tesla driver, who stopped and remained at the scene, no other drivers stopped. The CHP Solano Area office is asking that anyone who witnessed the accident or has any information contact them. Last week in a separate incident on I-80, a driver said he was asleep and using FSD when his Tesla plowed into a police car that was stopped at the scene of an accident. After that incident, CHP warned drivers that “Despite its name, full self-driving is not fully autonomous. Technology does not relieve drivers of their responsibility to safely operate their vehicles.”

articles.title: Tom Skerritt, Star of ‘Picket Fences’ and ‘Alien,’ Dies at 93
articles.summary: Mentored by Robert Altman in 'M*A*S*H,' the Emmy-winning actor later stood out in 'Top Gun,' 'The Turning Point' and 'A River Runs Through It.'
articles.body:
Tom Skerritt, the rough-hewn actor who sparkled amid ensembles in M*A*S*H , Alien and Top Gun before starring as small-town sheriff Jimmy Brock on the quirky 1990s series Picket Fences , has died. He was 93.

Skerritt died Wednesday in Seattle of natural causes, his family announced.

"We are heartbroken by his loss," they said. "While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humor, curiosity, wisdom, generosity and the love he brought into our lives. He cared deeply about imagination, creativity, storytelling, service, veterans, the natural world and helping others find and share their own voices."

The collaborative Skerritt also portrayed Shirley MacLaine's husband in the 11-time Oscar nominee The Turning Point (1977), was Tom Cruise's Air Force instructor Mike "Viper" Metcalf in Top Gun (1986) and was memorable as a minister and the patriarch of the MacLean family in Robert Redford 's rhythmic A River Runs Through It (1992).

Known for his outdoorsy features and bristly mustache, the handsome actor exuded masculinity during his six-decade career and was often cast in positions of authority — as when he starred as the iconic lawman Will Kane in a 2000 remake of High Noon for TBS.

Skerritt's breakthrough came in the 1970 feature M*A*S*H . As Southern surgeon Duke Forrest, he opens the film by stealing a jeep with co-conspirator Hawkeye Pierce ( Donald Sutherland ) to get them to the mobile hospital where they're assigned to treat injured U.S. soldiers during the Korean War.

Once there, the two join forces with Trapper John McIntrye (Elliott Gould) and set about questioning any rigid army regulation that stands in the way of their drinking and womanizing.

The anti-establishment, freewheeling comedy, directed by Robert Altman, was one of the year's most popular films and led to the long-running CBS series of the same name. Curiously, Skerritt's character was one of the few not included in the small-screen adaptation; nonetheless, the role proved the actor had star power.

The Detroit native credited Altman for giving him the freedom to create the character. "I just loved the guy from the first. He made me realize early on that you could do no wrong, as long as you tried," Skerritt said in Mitchell Zuckoff's 2009 book Robert Altman: The Oral Biography . "The worst you could do was make an ass out of yourself. And that's the first thing you have to be willing to do as an actor, be willing to make an ass out of yourself. Bob gave me that."

After his success with M*A*S*H , Skerritt began landing work in more films — Wild Rovers (1971), Fuzz (1972), Big Bad Mama (1974) and Ice Castles (1978) among them. He worked again with Altman in Thieves Like Us (1974) and did a zany turn in Cheech & Chong's Up in Smoke (1978) as Strawberry, a shell-shocked, pot-dealing Vietnam veteran .

Skerritt originally turned down the role as Captain Dallas of the doomed spacecraft Nostromo in Alien (1979) after fearing that the film's budget would be consumed by special effects. However, he reconsidered after learning that Ridley Scott had signed on to direct.

As Skerritt recalled in an interview for the 2001 TV documentary Alien Evolution , "Hold on here, let me see. I've heard of this Ridley Scott guy, I've heard that he did this thing called The Duellists [Scott's 1977 feature debut]. 'Can I see this?' And they said, 'Yes, we'll run a screening for you tomorrow.' So I went to see The Duellists . And it was a masterpiece. I mean, I have never seen a picture that captured so much production value as The Duellists . Magnificent-looking film, a painting from beginning to end. So I had to do Alien at that point."

For four seasons on CBS beginning in 1992, Skerritt starred on David E. Kelley's Picket Fences as the sheriff of the fictional Rome, Wisconsin, the voice of calm amid insanity. Skerritt, who played the husband of the town doctor (Kathy Baker) and a father of three, won the Emmy for outstanding lead actor in a drama series in 1993 and was nominated again the following year.

On the sixth season of Cheers , he portrayed Rebecca Howe's ( Kirstie Alley ) ultra-suave ex-boss, Evan Drake, and played Sally Field's deceased husband, William, on Brothers and Sisters . And he appeared as himself in a hilarious cameo in the 2012 comedy Ted .

And in 2021, he landed a rare leading role in a feature when he played a retired heart surgeon and recent widower who learns he has terminal cancer in East of the Mountains .

Thomas Roy Skerritt was born on Aug. 25, 1933, in the Motor City. After graduating from Mackenzie High School in 1951, he enlisted in the Air Force, hoping to see the world. Instead, lacking the skills to be a pilot, he spent most of his time in uniform in Austin as a classification specialist. Skerritt then returned to his hometown to study English at Wayne State University.

Deciding to pursue a career as a writer or director, Skerritt transferred to UCLA, where he also did some acting in a bid to overcome his shyness. He never dreamed he could make a living at it.

"I thought I would continue writing and continue acting if I was going to be a director," Skerritt told Film Comment in 2016. "I happened to be seen as an actor and I was hired for a little low-budget film and I thought, 'Hey, this is a great way to learn how to be a director, to be a participant in the actual reality of making a film.'

"You can't be a filmmaker purely by going to the university, as you know. The practical knowledge, the street knowledge you can gain by being on a set, being around that, being around the way people talk, the way they approach the business, was really the benefit I saw in it from the beginning."

The low-budget film was War Hunt (1962). Its producers, Terry and Denis Sanders, had seen Skerritt in a community stage production and offered him a job. The drama, featuring John Saxon , Sydney Pollack, Redford and Gavin MacLeod , was, like M*A*S*H , set during the Korean War.

Skerritt's on-camera appeal couldn't be denied, and he easily found more acting work. Throughout the 1960s, he appeared on episodes of Laramie , The Real McCoys , Alfred Hitchcock Presents , My Three Sons , Wagon Train , Voyage to the Bottom of the Sea , The Time Tunnel and Mannix .

The shows Death Valley Days , Gunsmoke , The F.B.I. , The Fugitive , 12 O'Clock High , Combat! , Bonanza and The Virginian showcased him multiple times in different roles.

After becoming friends with director Hal Ashby, Skerrit appeared in Harold and Maude (1971) as a motorcycle cop. (Skerritt stepped in to do the small role as a favor after an on-set accident caused an actor to bow out.) When asked about a credit, he chose to use Martin Bormann instead of his real name.

"We did silly things in those days, and we still do," he told Film Comment . "And I said, 'You know, Martin Bormann, second in command to Hitler, nobody ever found out what happened to that guy. Everyone else they were able to trace, but that guy just vanished.' I said, 'You know, I think he went to Oakland and became a motorcycle cop.' "

His other notable film credits included Savage Harvest (1981), The Dead Zone (1983), SpaceCamp (1986), Made to Order (1987), The Rookie (1990), Steel Magnolias (1989), Contact (1997), The Other Sister (1999), Tears of the Sun (2003), Bonneville (2006), Redemption Road (2010), A Hologram for the King (2016) and Day of Days (2017).

Skerritt also popped up on television on Kolchak: The Night Stalker , Cannon , Barnaby Jones , S.W.A.T. , Baretta , Chicago Hope , Will & Grace , The West Wing , The Grid , Law & Order: Special Victims Unit , Huff , Leverage , The Good Wife and Madam Secretary .

Survivors include his third wife, Julie Tokashiki, whom he married in 1998; his children, Andy, Erin, Matt, Collin and Emiko; grandchildren Sara, Maddison, Sunny, Louisa and Georgia; and great-grandchildren Marigold and Ravi.

Skerritt helped launch TheFilmSchool in Seattle to support the next generation of filmmakers and storytellers. That commitment extended to the Red Badge Project, which he co-founded to help veterans work through PTSD, anxiety and depression by writing and sharing their experiences.

His passion for service included protecting the natural world. Inspired in part by A River Runs Through It , he helped create and champion Reflections of the River, a documentary series exploring the health of America's rivers and the urgent need to protect them. He also supported river conservation through partnerships with the Wildlands Festival , American Rivers and the Gallatin River Task Force.

articles.title: Google tells Android users to update as parts of Canada adopt permanent daylight saving time
articles.summary: If you live in parts of Canada not turning the clock back on November 1st, Google suggests making sure your Android device is updated to avoid time issues.
articles.body: As the US gets closer to permanently adopting daylight saving time following the House advancing the Sunshine Protection Act in July, there could be some unforeseen consequences to getting an extra hour of sun in the evening all year long. Following the Canadian provinces of British Columbia and Manitoba permanently switching to daylight saving this year, Google has shared some suggested fixes if Android devices are showing the incorrect time when clocks aren’t turned back an hour there on November 1st. In an announcement shared to the Android community help forums, Google suggests a simple fix for Canadians experiencing issues as a result of recent time zone changes. “If you are in Canada and your device is showing an incorrect time due to the new time zone laws beginning Nov 1, please apply any pending updates from your phone’s manufacturer and Google, and then restart your device.” If your device is still displaying an incorrect time or time zone, Google suggests enabling location-based time zone detection by searching the “Date and Time” in Android’s settings and enabling both the “Automatic time zone” and “Use location for time zone” options. If all else fails, Google also suggests disabling “Automatic time zone” detection in the Android settings and manually selecting a time zone that matches the correct time offset for your region. While daylight saving time rules vary from province to province in Canada (and even within smaller regions) making it occasionally difficult for devices to stay on top of changes in a timely manner, it will potentially be less of an issue in the US if the entire country decides to adopt permanent daylight saving time all at once.

articles.title: Teenage Engineering launched an instrument amp with a ton of built-in effects
articles.summary: Teenage Engineering’s EP-35 is a battery-powered amp for your synths, guitar, and voice with tons of built-in effects and a camp light.
articles.body: Teenage Engineering is branching out into instrument amps with the previously leaked EP-35, a multi-input, multi-instrument, battery-powered amp with built-in effects. The back of the unit has a line-in port, as well as a 1/4-inch guitar input and an XLR input for mics, including mics that require phantom power. You can also stream audio to it via Bluetooth and connect multiple EP-35s together over Bluetooth using Auracast. If you have them paired in stereo, tilting a unit to the left or right sets it to the appropriate stereo channel, which is pretty neat. There are separate effects processors for guitar and vocals, though you have limited control over them. Instead of adding, say, a delay and dialing in the delay time, you pick a style-based preset like “blues,” “indie,” or “twang,” which applies a specific selection of effects, and you control the “amount” with a single knob. The vocal channel works the same way, but with different effects like “radio” and the all-essential “robo choir.” [Product: Teenage Engineering EP-35 amp | TE is also offering a number of accessories to pair with EP-35. The most interesting are the “amptenna,” which turns the unit into an FM radio, and the EP–127 KO Pedal. The pedal is a wireless MIDI controller that gives you additional control over the built-in effects, unlocks a simple looper and metronome, and includes an expression pedal jack which can be used to control the volume of a selected channel on the amp. And since the EP-127 also has a 3.5mm MIDI output and works as an HID controller, it can also be used with your other synths, pedals, or even to control video playback from your computer. The EP-35 amp is available now for $399.

articles.title: Mobile phone theft network spanning five states busted, 3 arrested
articles.summary: Dewas police bust five-state mobile theft racket; 3 arrested, 400 stolen smartphones worth Rs 1.5 crore and Rs 6 lakh cash recovered; smuggling probe on.
articles.body: Indore: What began as an investigation into a stolen mobile phone in Dewas led police to a mobile phone theft network spanning five states and 22 districts and the recovery of 400 stolen smartphones worth around Rs 1.5 crore and Rs 6 lakh in cash.Three men have been arrested and police are also probing suspected smuggling of the stolen devices abroad.The police investigation had started after 28-year-old Somesh Joshi, a resident of Jaishree Nagar in Dewas, reported that his Android phone had been stolen from his pocket while he was having breakfast at a food joint on AB Road on Sept 13. A case was registered at Kotwali police station on Sept 15 under a relevant section of the BNS.Dewas SP Puneet Gehlot said that the breakthrough came after police examined CCTV footage of two mobile thefts reported in the district. Tracking the suspects seen in the footage eventually led investigators from the local theft cases to a wider network involved in stealing, collecting and illegally trading mobile phones across multiple states.The accused were identified as Manish Pardi (26) of Khalayda village in Ujjain district, currently residing in Alwasa under Banganga police station in Indore; Suraj Singh Pardi (30) also of Khalayda village; and Shubham Rathore (28) of Transport Nagar and Rishi Palace in Dwarkapuri, Indore. Rathore has allegedly been identified as the main receiver in the network.A special team led by Kotwali inspector Shashikant Chaurasia was formed and police subsequently widened the investigation from the persons allegedly carrying out the thefts to those collecting the stolen phones and arranging their illegal buying and sale. According to police, gang members targeted crowded markets, railway stations and other public places.The SP said that the investigation first led police to Manish Pardi, whose interrogation revealed that he was in contact with a man in Dwarkapuri through a WhatsApp number. The number was switched off, prompting police to conduct an IPDR (Internet Protocol Detail Records) analysis, which led them to Shubham Rathore’s number. A search of Rathore’s house resulted in the recovery of 400 smartphones, including Android phones of different brands and iPhones, estimated to be worth Rs 1.5 crore besides Rs 6 lakh in cash.Police found that Rathore had travelled to Bengal, Bihar and Nepal over the past six to seven months. He reportedly works as a halwai and prepares food, but investigators are now examining his movements and contacts to establish the wider network. Rathore is currently on remand.Investigators believe the network is much larger than what the profiles of the arrested accused initially suggested. The network has been linked to Dewas, Indore, Ujjain, Dhar and Chhatarpur in Madhya Pradesh; Mumbai-Thane, Nashik, Kolhapur, Jalgaon, Jalna, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar and Ahilyanagar in Maharashtra; Ahmedabad, Vadodara, Bharuch, Navsari and Dahej in Gujarat; Jaipur and Ajmer in Rajasthan; and Daman.Police said stolen phones were transported through different channels to Rathore in Indore. He allegedly acted as the main receiver, collecting the devices and arranging their further illegal sale.During the investigation, police also found information suggesting that phones collected in Indore may have been supplied abroad through other agents. Investigators are questioning the accused to establish the suspected international smuggling route and identify others involved in the network. The individual devices are being verified to establish their original theft cases and the complete supply chain through which they reached the accused.Rathore has eight previous cases listed against him, including theft, burglary, receiving stolen property, an Arms Act case and cases involving assault and intimidation registered at Tukoganj, Vijay Nagar, Dwarkapuri, Annapurna, Tejajinagar and Chandan Nagar police stations in Indore.Suraj Singh has two previous cases registered at Ghatiya police station in Ujjain. Manish Pardi has a previous case under the Arms Act registered at Raghvi police station in Ujjain.BOXRemain cautious, advise copsDewas police have appealed to people to remain cautious with mobile phones and other valuables in crowded markets and public places. Police have advised people not to buy second-hand phones from unknown persons without verifying ownership and a valid bill. In case of mobile theft, people have been advised to immediately report it to the nearest police station and use the Sanchar Saathi portal to block the stolen device. Suspicious activity can also be reported on Dial-112.PointersHow the case UnfoldedProbe starts with case of one stolen mobile phone in DewasCCTV footage helped police trace the suspects and arrest Manish Pardi.Pardi revealed a Dwarkapuri contact; IPDR analysis of a switched-off WhatsApp number led police to Shubham RathoreSearch at Rathore’s house resulted in the recovery of stolen phones,Police suspect stolen phones were being collected in Indore & may have been routed through agents for smuggling abroadYou Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Indore | Silver Rate in Indore | Bank Holidays in Indore | Public Holidays in Indore | Petrol Price in Indore | Diesel Price in Indore | CNG Price in Indore | LPG Price in IndoreStay updated with the latest Indore news. articles.title: PC shipments dropped over 20 percent in Q3 due to RAM price hikes
articles.summary: Counterpoint Research says global PC shipments fell 21 percent in Q3 2026, driven by price hikes for RAM and other components.
articles.body: Demand for new PCs took a hit after months of price hikes, with Counterpoint Research reporting global PC shipments fell 21 percent year-over-year in Q3 2026. That’s in line with earlier reports from IDC and Omdia. It’s not just PCs, either — that same quarter, smartphone shipments also hit a 14-year low. Counterpoint linked the decline in PC shipments to higher component prices. Up until Q2 2026, PC shipments had been growing for over two years straight. But over the last several months, RAM, SSDs, and chips from Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm have all gotten more expensive, leading to price hikes on everything from MacBooks to Raspberry Pis. Counterpoint senior analyst Minsoo Kang noted that some companies are shifting to “prioritize configurations that can better absorb component inflation,” leaving fewer affordable options for price-sensitive buyers. Some companies are even reviving older tech, like DDR4 RAM and 4GB GPUs, to help mitigate price hikes. Counterpoint also says Q3 2025 included “purchases ahead of the Windows 10 support deadline and tariff-related inventory adjustments,” which added to the sharp year-over-year drop this past quarter. The PC market might not bounce back anytime soon, as Counterpoint associate director David Naranjo says, “With global shipments expected to plunge 27% in Q4 2026 and remain broadly flat in 2027, stabilization should not be mistaken for recovery.”
